headline: In six months, nobody will remember why you made this decision.

slides.html:
In six months, nobody will remember why you made this decision.

Architecture Decision Records: the cheapest architecture practice that actually works.

A new engineer joins

“Why are we using a queue here instead of a direct call?”

Nobody knows. The person who decided left last year. The reasoning lived in a meeting and a Slack thread.

So the team has two bad options:

Blindly keep it — and stay stuck with a choice that may no longer fit.

Blindly change it — and rediscover the problem it was solving.

Michael Nygard · 2011

One decision. One short file. Five parts.

TitleShort, numberedStatusProposed, accepted, supersededContextThe forces at playDecisionWhat we will doConsequencesWhat gets easier, and harder

Stored as markdown in the repo, next to the code it describes.

Never edit history. Supersede it.

The old record stays. Anyone can trace how the thinking changed — and why.

Illustrative ADR
# 014. Order events via a queue
Status: Accepted
Context: Checkout calls 4 services synchronously. A slow inventory call fails the whole order at peak.
Decision: Publish an OrderPlaced event. Downstream services consume it asynchronously.
Consequences:
+ Checkout no longer waits on inventory
− Eventual consistency; need idempotent consumers and a dead-letter queue

One page. Twenty minutes to write. Years of saved arguments.

When to write one

Ask: would this be expensive to reverse, or confusing to someone new?

✓  Database, queue or cloud service choice
✓  Sync vs async between services
✓  Auth, tenancy or data-retention model
✓  Build vs buy
✗  Library minor versions, naming, lint rules

Review ADRs in pull requests, like code. The discussion is the decision.

Remember this

Code shows what you built. Only a record explains why.

Write the consequences honestly — including what gets harder.

Short and kept beats complete and abandoned.

Which decision in your system does nobody remember the reason for?

Tell me in the comments — and whether you'd keep it today.
